To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the emissions of local pollutants in US metropolitan areas scale according to a power law with both city size and gross domestic production; (ii) the monetary damages from the local air pollution in US metropolitan areas also scale according to a similar power law with city size and gross production; (iii) in metropolitan areas out of attainment with local air quality standards, the local air pollution emissions scale according to a different power law with city population, and the monetary damages from air pollution also scale according to different

(1) local air emissions scale according to a three-fourth power law with both metropolitan population size and gross metropolitan product (GDP) in the United states between 1999-2011; (2) the monetary damages from air emissions scale according a linear relationship with both metropolitan population and GDP; (3) counties out of attainment with local air quality standards show an entirely different scaling relationship: emissions scale according to square root of population and damages scale according to a two-thirds power law

1) the scaling relationships between population, emissions, and economic growth differ between MSAs in attainment and out of attainment with local air quality standards and 2) the relationship between emissions and damages is non-linear in all MSAs.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how the scaling relationships between urban population, economic output, and emissions change in response to environmental regulation.
the link between urban growth, economic growth, and the environment.
the relationship between population size, economic activity, and environmental quality in cities.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
“Environmental policy does not affect scaling laws between emissions, population and pollution, but does affect scaling laws between damages, population and pollution.
environmental policies can limit the adverse effects of city size on the local environment, while at the same time not limiting the productivity benefits that come from cities.
“Environmental regulation limits the adverse effects associated with urbanization, but does not interfere with the productivity benefits of cities.”
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
environmental regulation is effective at reducing local emissions, but it does so without reducing the economic growth benefits of urbanization.
the scaling relationships between pollution, population and economic growth can change as a result of environmental policy.
urbanization and economic growth are not inherently harmful to the environment and can be regulated to be environmentally benign.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the scaling laws between pollution and population are not universal.
environmental regulation may not be as costly as commonly assumed, and may actually be a key factor in the success of cities.
the relationship between emissions, damages and population is not universal and that environmental policy can change this relationship.
